title: Silver Cliff Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Silver Cliff wells have a 225 ft median depth, with fractured-bedrock drilling commonly priced by the foot.
h1: Silver Cliff, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Silver Cliff means dealing mostly with fractured mountain bedrock rather than a predictable basin aquifer. Records for permitted wells within 5 miles show a median depth of 225 feet, a median reported yield of 7.5 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 80 feet.

Those figures describe nearby permits, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Ground can change quickly across the mountain terrain. Before buying or building, review neighboring well logs, confirm the intended use with Colorado DWR, and get a driller's opinion based on the exact parcel.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Silver Cliff?
sections.html:
The median permitted well near Silver Cliff is 225 feet deep. The middle half runs from 150 to 325 feet, which is the most useful range when you are asking for a preliminary drilling bid. A contractor quoting only the median may understate the risk on a difficult parcel.

Depths vary substantially in this fractured granite and gneiss setting. About 54% of reported wells are between 100 and 300 feet, while 30% fall between 300 and 600 feet. The record includes a well at 1,345 feet, and 4% are deeper than 600 feet. Nearby Westcliffe may provide useful context, but the adjacent well log is more valuable than a regional average.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Silver Cliff well make?
sections.html:
Reported pump yield has a median of 7.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for many household uses, but the number is a tested or reported well result, not a promise for a new hole.

Most reported wells, 65%, produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 13% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Low-yield wells still occur: 19% are in the 1-to-5-gallon range and 3% are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask how a driller handles storage, pump sizing, and a low-producing fracture before you rely on the median.

sections.heading: Is the water table changing near Silver Cliff?
sections.html:
Static water level is the distance from the ground surface down to the water when the well is not being pumped. Among records that report it, the median is 80 feet, with the middle half from 60 to 140 feet.

The decade comparison deserves attention. The median measured water level was 68 feet below surface in the 2010s and 100 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels in the newer decade, although the records may represent different locations, seasons, well types, and measurement conditions. It is not enough by itself to prove a uniform decline across Silver Cliff. Have the seller provide recent pumping and water-level information for the specific well.

sections.heading: Who has drilled wells near Silver Cliff, and when?
sections.html:
The permit history shows sustained drilling activity, with the largest decade totals in the 1990s and 2000s. Records list 413 permits from the 1990s, 318 from the 2000s, 156 from the 2010s, and 153 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

In the records, Nequette Drilling, also listed as Nequette, David J., has 457 wells; Arkansas Valley Drilling, listed as Moore, Todd A., has 245; and Finney Drilling, listed as Finney, Larry D., has 128. These are the most active names in this dataset, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, and the exact scope of a bid before hiring.

sections.heading: What does it cost to drill a well in Silver Cliff?
sections.html:
Here, the ground is described as fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. A typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 225 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $14,600 to $22,500.

That is not the complete water-system price. A finished well with a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $20,600 to $34,500 at the median depth. Fractured rock can require deeper drilling before a productive water-bearing zone is found, so ask what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected. Get separate line items for casing, grout, pump equipment, power work, trenching, testing, and any difficult access.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building on a mountain lot
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The mapped area has 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,982 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped features do not prove contamination at a property, but they justify a proper water test and review of nearby land uses, mine history, and well construction.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, covering 1,632 wells; only 2 name Quaternary Alluvium, and no wells name a Denver Basin aquifer. Check casing and grout, well setbacks, septic placement, and the proposed building footprint together. A septic system, access route, and house location may need to be planned around rock, slope, drainage, and the well's protection area.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Silver Cliff: a practical check
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction record for the property, then compare it with nearby wells in Silver Cliff, Westcliffe, and other relevant parts of Custer County. Confirm the well's permitted use, tested yield, static level, pump details, and whether the records describe a completed well or only a permit.

For a vacant parcel, have a driller assess access, likely bedrock, siting, and the consequences of a low-yield or dry hole before you remove a contract contingency. A household well may be an exempt-use well, but the permit terms still control. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Treat the well, septic system, driveway, and house as one site-design problem rather than separate projects.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Silver Cliff, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Silver Cliff is 225 feet. The middle half runs from 150 to 325 feet, while 30% are between 300 and 600 feet. The record reaches 1,345 feet, so a local median is useful for planning but cannot cap the risk on a particular fractured-bedrock parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Silver Cliff?
faq.a: The drilling rate used for Silver Cliff is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 225-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $14,600 to $22,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,600 to $34,500. Difficult access or deeper drilling can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a well make in Silver Cliff?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 7.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. About 3% of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, while 19% produce from 1 to 5 gallons per minute. Ask for the actual well test and storage plan.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Silver Cliff?
faq.a: Nearby records include 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,982 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These findings do not establish contamination on your property. Test the well water for relevant contaminants, review nearby mine and land-use history, and check casing and grout condition.

faq.q: Should I drill a well before building near Silver Cliff?
faq.a: For a vacant lot, investigate the well before committing to house and septic construction. The local median static water level is 80 feet, but the middle half is 60 to 140 feet, and fractured granite or gneiss can produce uneven results. Confirm the DWR permit, intended use, access, septic siting, and a driller's plan for low yield or a dry hole.
